candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year. The mission ended abruptly 14 months ahead of its planned end date when scientists lost contact with the probe . An Indian PSLV rocket launches the Chandrayaan-1 moon mission on Oct. 21, 2008 EDT (Oct. 22 local time in India). (Image credit: ISRO) Why it mattered The Indian Space Research Organisation , or ISRO, had a lot riding on the success of Chandrayaan-1 moon mission, which marked the first-ever deep space mission by the Indian space agency. It was also the first mission to the moon for India, a country that hopes to launch its own crewed spacecraft and build a space station. Chandrayaan-1 did more than just demonstrate that India's space program was capable of launching missions to the moon; it also returned some amazing science results, like evidence of water ice on the moon . candidates.title: Orionid meteor shower peaks tonight: Here's the best time to spot shooting stars
candidates.raw_excerpt: Don't miss the Orionid meteor shower peak tonight (Oct. 21-22) as tiny shards of Halley's Comet collide with Earth's atmosphere to carve fiery streaks through the Autumn sky! But will the light cast by the waxing gibbous moon spoil the show? The Orionid meteor shower activity peaks when Earth travels through the densest section of the debris trail left by Comet 1P/Halley. The comet is currently racing back towards the sun ahead of its next visit to the inner solar system in 2061. Under perfect dark sky conditions 10 to 20 shooting stars could brighten the night sky each hour as the peak unfolds, according to NASA . However, the light cast by the waxing moon — just four days from being full — will likely reduce the number of visible meteors by hiding fainter Orionids from sight. Orionid shooting stars will appear to travel away from a point of origin, close to the red star Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion , rising above the eastern horizon an hour before midnight for viewers in the U.S. When and where to see Orionid shooting stars this October Your best chance at spotting the fast-moving meteors will come in the hours before dawn on Oct. 22, after the moon has set and the radiant approaches its highest point in the night sky. It's best not to stare directly at the radiant, where the glowing meteor trails will be relatively short compared to those left by shooting stars that appear 45-90 degrees away from the bright star Betelgeuse, thanks to an effect known as foreshortening. candidates.raw_excerpt:
A CERES-1S Y8 carrier rocket blasted off at 11:39 am Beijing time on Wednesday from waters near east China's Shandong Province, delivering the Xiguang-4 01 satellite into a 541 km-altitude low Earth orbit.

Xiguang-4 01 is the pilot satellite of the Wuyang Constellation, the world's first low-inclination remote sensing constellation. After entering orbit, Xiguang-4 01 will mainly provide commercial remote sensing services for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, South China, and low-latitude regions along the Maritime Silk Road. Its support functions will include natural resource monitoring, agricultural production, marine observation, ecological protection, flood and typhoon emergency response, disaster mitigation and urban governance.

Developed by Galactic Energy, the CERES-1 rocket model is China's first commercial rocket model capable of launching from both land and sea platforms. Wednesday's launch was the seventh sea launch mission of the CERES-1S carrier rocket. Since its maiden flight on September 5, 2023, the CERES-1S has maintained a 100% launch success rate.

candidates.title: China to build world's first deep-sea floating island
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China is to build the world's first floating artificial island for all-weather, long-term deep-sea scientific research. Under a contract signed in Shanghai, the project will be undertaken by Shanghai Jiao Tong University and constructed by Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding, a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), the world's largest shipbuilding group.

As the world's first ultra-large marine scientific research platform, the artificial island is being designed to withstand extreme sea conditions and maintain long-term presence in the open ocean, while also offering rapid mobility and deployment. It will serve as a research base for frontier studies in marine science, marine equipment, and marine meteorology.

The large scientific facility will comprise three main systems: the main facility platform, ship-based laboratories, and shore-based support. The main facility platform will have a "semi-submersible twin-hull" design. It will be 138 meters long, 85 meters wide, with a main deck height of 45 meters. It's set to sustain sea state 7 conditions and safely survive a category 17 typhoon.

The order to build the facility is worth 2.76 billion yuan (about 413 million US dollars). Developed as a national major science and technology infrastructure project, Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding is expected to begin construction in 2028, with delivery due in June, 2030.

Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle."

He said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing.

Zond 8 was considered a success — even though its guidance system malfunctioned on the way back to Earth. The Soviet Union's Zond 8 spacecraft, the last in a series of lunar spacecraft, captured this image of Earthrise on Oct. 24, 1970. candidates.title: Starwatch: Orionid meteor shower to peak on night skies
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The annual Orionid meteor shower is set to peak on the night of October 21 to 22, offering stargazers a chance to witness one of the major meteor showers of the year. Around 20 meteors can be seen per hour under ideal viewing conditions.

The Orionids are active each year from October 2 to November 7. With a rate of about 10 to 20 meteors per hour, they are considered to be one of the most beautiful showers of the year, according to NASA.

The meteor shower is created by dust and debris left behind by Comet 1P/Halley. As Earth travels along its orbit around the sun, it passes through particles shed by the comet during its journeys through the inner solar system. These tiny particles collide with Earth's atmosphere at extremely high speeds, producing the bright streaks of light known as meteors.

As Earth crosses different parts of this debris stream twice each year, the dust grains become two annual meteor showers – the Orionids in October and the Eta Aquariids in May.

Armenian Environment Minister Hambardzum Matevosyan was elected COP17 president for a two-year term at the plenary.

candidates.title: Japan launches mission to return samples from Mars moon
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Japan launched an uncrewed spacecraft toward the Martian moon Phobos on Tuesday on a mission intended to become the first to collect samples from the small, rocky body and return them to Earth for analysis.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft lifted off aboard an H3 rocket before dawn from the Tanegashima Space Center in southwestern Japan.

The spacecraft is expected to reach Mars in August 2027 and return the samples to Earth in 2031. JAXA hopes the mission will shed light on the origin of the two Martian moons and deepen our understanding of the solar system's early stages.

Phobos, the larger of the two moons, orbits Mars three times a day. It has an irregular shape with dimensions of about 27 km by 22 km by 18 km, and it orbits roughly 6,000 km above the Martian surface.

JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of material from the surface to return to Earth for analysis.

The launch marked the first interplanetary mission for Japan's H3 rocket. The country's flagship launcher experienced a high-profile failure on its inaugural flight in 2023 when its second-stage engine failed to ignite, but it has since completed a series of mostly successful launches.

candidates.title: JAXA’s MMX Enroute to Mars To Return Samples of Phobos
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency successfully launch the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission this afternoon EDT. MMX will not land on Mars, but instead explore its two moons, Phobos and Deimos, returning samples of Phobos to Earth in 2031. Japan and the U.S. have returned samples of asteroids, but this will be the first from a moon other than our own and could solve the mystery of whether Phobos is an asteroid captured by Mars’s gravity or a piece of Mars ejected by a collision. MMX lifted off on a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries H3 rocket at 3:41 pm EDT today, Monday, October 19, 2026 — the early hours (4:41 am) of Tuesday, October 20, at the Tanegashima launch site. Liftoff of JAXA’s Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft from Tanegashima, Japan, October 19, 2026 EDT (October 20 local time in Japan). Screenshot from JAXA webcast . MMX is headed to Mars, but instead of landing it will enter a Quasi-Satellite Orbit or QSO. That will enable it study the moons Phobos and Deimos including a landing on Phobos to collect samples for return to Earth. The two small moons are a scientific mystery. The larger of the two, Phobos, is just 22 kilometers (14 miles) in diameter. Deimos is even smaller, 12 km (7.5 mi). Are they asteroids captured by the gravity of Mars, or ejecta from a collision between Mars and another celestial object eons ago? The asteroid belt with its millions of asteroids — rocks left over from the formation of the solar system — lies between Mars and Jupiter. But the orbits of Phobos and Deimos are circular and aligned with Mars’s equator, not tilted. That suggests to others they weren’t randomly pulled into orbit around Mars, but instead that an impact on Mars might have ejected material into orbit where it collected into these moons. NASA rendering of Phobos and Deimos orbiting Mars. Credit: NASA Today’s launch was just the first leg of the journey, which will last five years. MMX will arrive at Mars in August 2027 and descend to land on Phobos

candidates.title: Russian spacecraft maneuvers in "extreme proximity" to satellite used by Ukraine
candidates.raw_excerpt: A Russian military satellite maneuvered in "extreme proximity" of a commercial Earth-imaging satellite in recent days in the first known example an unsanctioned rendezvous in low-Earth orbit, according to the orbital intelligence company LeoLabs. The Russian spacecraft, Kosmos 2612, "conducted a deliberate series of maneuvers toward ICEYE-X36, a US-operated commercial imaging satellite," LeoLabs said. "Kosmos 2612 closed from hundreds of kilometers away to extreme proximity to ICEYE-X36. It then maneuvered around ICEYE-X36, remained nearby for an extended period, and then began moving away." US military officials and independent analysts have tracked Kosmos 2612 since its April launch on a Soyuz rocket from a spaceport in northern Russia. Within weeks, it became apparent that at least four of the six satellites from that launch were stalking ICEYE-X36 after they adjusted orbits to line up with the orbit of the ICEYE spacecraft. candidates.title: Political Candidates Spending An Obscene Amount of Money on AI-Generated Election Slop
candidates.raw_excerpt: Whether as short-form slop Reels or the data centers that spit them out, Americans are absolutely sick of AI . Their elected officials, however, are going all-in — both embracing gobs of money from tech lobbying arms, and increasingly even embracing the tech to churn out attack ads to tarnish their opponents. According to reporting from the New York Times , AI generated election ads have become a hundred-million dollar business, generating over $137 million in promotional revenue already in the current election cycle. That’s nearly a quarter of all spending on midterm political advertising overall — which amounts to a cool $565 million in spending across all US house and senate campaigns, according to Wesleyan University’s Wesleyan Media Project research lab. To date, Wesleyan media researchers found that political action groups have generated over 220 midterm election ads with AI. The vast majority, or 80 percent of those are made by Republicans, with 20 percent generated by Democrats. For example, one ad by Make Oklahoma Great Again shows Republican candidate for Oklahoma governor Mike Mazzei embracing an AI-version of Hillary Clinton, while an AI Donald Trump pouts off to the side. “Clinton lover, Trump hater,” the ad intones. “That’s Mike Mazzei.” The ad contains no mention that it was generated by AI. As the NYT notes, the PAC has spent over $200,000 buying TV ad time for the AI commercial across the state of Oklahoma. “I think what we’re seeing with AI has surprised even us,” professor of government and co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project Erika Franklin Fowler told the NYT . “Some of the ways in which AI is used, honestly, if there wasn’t a disclaimer on the ad, it would be hard to know that AI was there.” More on AI: OpenAI Hit With Stack of Lawsuits Over ChatGPT Allegedly Coaching Children to Harm Themselves The post Political Candidates Spending An Obscene Amount of Money on AI-Generated Election Slop appeared first on Futurism .

candidates.title: OHB Wins ESA Study Deal for Lunar Infrastructure
candidates.raw_excerpt: OHB has won a new lunar infrastructure deal from the European Space Agency (ESA). Its subsidiary, OHB System AG, has won a feasibility and preliminary design studies deal for OASIS — the Outpost for Advanced Scientific Investigation Station — a shared infrastructure planned support scientific experiments and technology demonstrations on the lunar surface over the long term. OHB announced the deal, Oct. 19. As prime contractor for the ESA studies, OHB is responsible for the overall system concept and is working together with partners on system requirements and the preliminary design phase. OASIS is envisioned to be a modular and scalable concept to support a variety of scientific instruments, technology demonstrators and robotic systems in the future. The OASIS concept is compared to the role of research stations or utility networks on Earth. Future lunar payloads could rely on shared infrastructure and central services instead of having to develop and transport power, communications and data systems for every mission separately. The OASIS platform is designed to provide core services such as power supply, communications and data storage for multiple payloads, thereby enabling long-term scientific and technological activities on the lunar surface. “With OASIS, we are taking lunar exploration a step further. Europe is not only looking at individual missions to the Moon, but at the infrastructure that will enable long-term scientific research and technological innovation in the first place. With OASIS, we are creating the conditions that will allow science and technology activities to be conducted on the lunar surface sustainably and beyond the scope of individual missions,” Marco Fuchs, CEO, OHB, said in a statement. The post OHB Wins ESA Study Deal for Lunar Infrastructure appeared first on Via Satellite .

The JAXA ( Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency )-led MMX mission is bound for Mars orbit, where it will study the planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos. If everything goes according to plan, MMX will become the first spacecraft to land on and return samples from Phobos for study back on Earth, which scientists think could shed light on a decades-old mystery about the moons' origins and reveal clues about the formation of the early solar system . a rocket launches into a night sky from a seaside pad (Image credit: JAXA) It was the 10th liftoff of Japan's expendable, two-stage H3 rocket, which was jointly developed by JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. After clearing its launch pad today, the 207-foot-tall (63 meters) launch vehicle flew a nominal trajectory through its ascent corridor over the Pacific Ocean, jettisoning its four solid boosters in pairs just before the flight clock reached two minutes. H3's first stage, powered by two LE-9 rocket engines, channels a mixture of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to produce a combined thrust of 331,000 pounds (1,471 kN), according to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. But something went wrong during the lander's descent, and it crashed into the ground. Schiaparelli did not survive the accident , but the Trace Gas Orbiter is still functional. It is currently circling the planet, looking for methane and other gases in the Martian atmosphere that could be evidence for possible biological activity. candidates.raw_excerpt: Over the last few days, a Russian satellite deliberately maneuvered within “extreme proximity” of an Iceye satellite, according to space domain awareness data provider LeoLabs. Russia’s COSMOS 2612 began moving closer to ICEYE-X36 on Oct. 15, LeoLabs detailed in an event report released Monday. The satellite began to transition away on Oct. 18 and 19 with LeoLabs confirming that close proximity activity ended. Iceye is “aware of the situation and tracking it closely,” a spokesperson said in a statement to Via Satellite . “Our constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience.” LeoLabs stated this shows how commercial satellites are operating a “contested and strategically important environment,” while noting the observations do not establish hostile intent. “These actions require planning, maneuverability, precise navigation, and significant fuel. candidates.title: Truth Social Stock Hits All-Time Low as Userbase Craters on Trump’s Twitter Clone
candidates.raw_excerpt: Donald Trump’s Twitter clone, Truth Social, is in serious trouble. The company has weathered bad news before, hitting all-time low stock prices on multiple occasions over the past year. But those days now look balmy in comparison, with the social network’s shares sliding more than 7.5 percent on Monday alone and setting a new rock bottom of just $6.40. Zooming out doesn’t paint a prettier picture, either: over the past month, the company’s stock has fallen a stomach-churning 29 percent. It’s easy to empathize with any investors looking to ditch the company. It never had much of a raison d’être beyond “funnel some money to Trump,” and the president’s declining political fortunes — not to mention looming midterms that are likely to undermine his remaining power — have weakened even that grift-era pitch. As the Daily Beast reported last week , not even its users are sticking around, with analytics data suggesting that its daily traffic has cratered by more than 30 percent over the past year. For a company that was already posting huge losses every quarter , that’s grim news — and it sounds like the company’s remaining investors may now be seeing the writing on the wall. As its fortunes have soured, Truth Social has tried a series of eyebrow-raising pivots into gambling and crypto that failed to gain traction . It also moved to merge with a nuclear fusion company and started selling early access to Trump’s messages on the platform, in a move that was widely derided as an attempt to profit off his position as president. So far, none of those moves have showed any signs of turning around the company’s fortunes. Add it all up, and it’s hard not to wonder whether Truth Social will survive as long as Trump’s second administration. candidates.title: The moon is shrinking. 10,000 cracks on the lunar surface reveal by how much
candidates.raw_excerpt: The moon is shrinking, and scientists are narrowing in on exactly how much our natural satellite has dwindled over the years. The moon is thought to have formed from a violent collision between a massive object and our young Earth roughly 4.5 billion years ago, and its interior is still gradually cooling off from this ancient collision. As it cools, the moon contracts, leading to a long, slow shrinking process . Now, in a new study, scientists think that they have figured out how much smaller the moon is actually getting. In this new study, scientists analyzing images snapped by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) have spotted over 10,000 young faults, or cracks across the moon's surface. This helped them to figure out how much the moon has contracted over time, and they now estimate that the moon's radius has decreased by about 148 feet (45 meters) over the past 400 to 800 million years. "The number of these young faults revealed in LROC images is much greater than I ever imagined," study lead Thomas Watters, a geologist and scientist emeritus at the Center for Earth and Planetary Studies at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum, said in a statement . "As the interior of the moon continues to cool and contract, it is expected that the growth of existing faults and formation of new faults continues today." Lobate scarps on the lunar surface, as seen by LROC. (Image credit: NASA/KARI/ASU/Intuitive Machines/Smithsonian ) With these LROC observations, researchers in this study saw a variety of different types of cracks and landforms across the lunar surface. candidates.raw_excerpt: Fears of an AI bubble have been growing for years. And now the International Monetary Fund is the latest to sound the alarm. In its Global Financial Stability Report published last week , the global financial institution warned that markets everywhere are increasingly at the mercy of precarious AI investments. The untold billions poured into AI has driven economic growth, the IMF says, but the boom could quickly invert if profits, which so far have largely proven elusive, never come to fruition — or at least not proportionately with the epic investment levels. AI stocks would tank, and the resulting market correction would send powerful shocks across the global economy. “Growing leverage could be a catalyst for such a correction,” the IMF warned in a blog post about its findings. “Hyperscalers, as the largest data center operators are known, are borrowing more and more, while investors have been leveraging to invest in AI stocks.” The report also casts a wary eye to the circular nature of AI financing , in which the biggest benefactors and beneficiaries of AI companies are other AI companies. candidates.title: 78-Year-Old Woman Hauled Off In Handcuffs After Blocking Delivery Robot
candidates.raw_excerpt: A retired professor was handcuffed and arrested last week, for the crime of standing on the sidewalk in front of a delivery robot. According to local channel 6ABC , 78-year-old Carolyn Marvin was arrested in Philadelphia’s Center City, after planting her feet in the path of an oncoming Avride delivery robot. Marvin, a retired communications professor at the University of Pennsylvania, told local reporters she was protesting the robots due to the threat they pose to local delivery workers. “I know they’re taking the jobs of human delivery workers,” Marvin told 6ABC , “and so I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward.” The “confrontation” — if you can call it that — attracted a small crowd, who watched as police ordered Marvin to move out of the robot’s path. When she refused, citing protected speech, she was arrested and charged with one count of disorderly conduct, which she reportedly plans to dispute in court. It wasn’t Marvin’s first time passively protesting Philadelphia’s growing fleet of delivery robots, and it probably won’t be her last. Asked by 6ABC whether she plans on continuing her demonstrations, she replied that “I do. Why not?” “I think it’s my First Amendment right to publicly demonstrate on a sidewalk to protest against delivery robots,” Marvin continued. In a separate interview with KYW Newsradio , the retired professor said she was protesting the “ruthless way that rich corporations are casting aside human workers — and here, we’re talking about the humble delivery folks — in order to enrich their bottom lines.” The incident raises a valid legal question around delivery bots: if the privately-owned devices need unimpeded access to public infrastructure to work, who’s responsible for making sure they have room to roam?
